title: How far can we push computing?
gist: Gurses argues that Moore's, Dennard's and related scaling laws are slowing, forcing AI-era progress to come from brute-force buildout (over $700 billion hyperscaler capex) even though fundamental physical limits lie 6 to 35 orders of magnitude away. Energy per operation and communication are the nearest floors, with reversible logic and co-packaged optics as early routes.

insights.claim: Six of the biggest hyperscalers are on track to spend more than $700 billion this year on computing infrastructure, about twice their 2025 record, building faster than the electrical grid can feed the sites.
insights.speaker: Volkan Gurses
insights.so_what: Capex is brute-force performance buying, with grid power as the binding constraint.
insights.quote: are on track to spend more than $700 billion this year on computing infrastructure

insights.claim: Moore's, Dennard's, Koomey's, Kryder's and Keck's laws are all slowing or ending, so the engineering gains that drove 20th-century computing are fading.
insights.speaker: Volkan Gurses
insights.so_what: Chip-level improvement is no longer a free tailwind for compute-intensive business models.
insights.quote: Moore’s Law, which plots how densely transistors can be constructed on silicon, has slowed down

insights.claim: Scaling laws are observations about engineered systems, not physical laws, and the true physical limits of computing lie far below anything in a data center today.
insights.speaker: Volkan Gurses
insights.so_what: Stalling of trend lines is an engineering problem, not a physics wall.
insights.quote: But these scaling laws are merely observations about systems that we have engineered; they are not fundamental physical laws.

insights.claim: Dennard scaling ended around 2004 when chips could no longer shed heat; clock speeds stalled near three gigahertz, Intel canceled its four-gigahertz processor, and the industry pivoted to multicore.
insights.speaker: Volkan Gurses
insights.so_what: Heat, not transistor size, ended single-core speed gains and shifted progress to system scale-out.
insights.quote: Around 2004, though, the gift ran out.

insights.claim: Progress is now bought mostly by scaling the whole system (more chips, memory, power and cooling) rather than shrinking the transistor; each new chip generation arrives more slowly and pays back less in speed and power.
insights.speaker: Volkan Gurses
insights.so_what: Returns shift toward interconnect, power, packaging and cooling suppliers rather than node shrinks.
insights.quote: Progress is now bought mostly by scaling up the system

insights.claim: AI training compute has doubled roughly every six months since 2010, far faster than Moore's Law allows, with little of that progress due to shrinking.
insights.speaker: Volkan Gurses
insights.so_what: AI capability growth is a spending and system-scale story, which compounds power demand.
insights.quote: has doubled roughly every six months since 2010

insights.claim: Transistor density has grown 10 orders of magnitude, speed 12 orders, and energy per operation has fallen 17 orders of magnitude, from about 100 joules for a vacuum-tube machine to about a femtojoule per logic-gate switch.
insights.speaker: Volkan Gurses
insights.so_what: Shows how far the historical descent went before the limits are even approached.
insights.quote: energy per operation has fallen 17 orders of magnitude

insights.claim: Seth Lloyd's 'ultimate laptop' (one kilogram in one liter) could run about 5x10^50 operations per second, some 35 orders of magnitude faster than a leading chip today, but would be a plasma at about a billion degrees.
insights.speaker: Volkan Gurses
insights.so_what: Computing speed has the largest gap to its limit, and is the least bridgeable.
insights.quote: Spend all of that on computation, and the ultimate laptop runs at roughly 5 ×1050 operations per second

insights.claim: Landauer's limit sets about 2.9x10^-21 joules to erase a bit at room temperature; today's chips spend several hundred thousand times more per switch, and sit less than six orders of magnitude above it.
insights.speaker: Volkan Gurses
insights.so_what: Energy per operation is the nearest floor, so efficiency gains are physically possible but finite.
insights.quote: Erasing a single bit must release a minimum quantity of heat

insights.claim: The Bekenstein bound caps memory at about 10^42 bits for a region the size of Lloyd's laptop, nearly 30 orders of magnitude beyond what a device that size stores today.
insights.speaker: Volkan Gurses
insights.so_what: Storage density has huge theoretical headroom, constrained by fabrication.
insights.locator: Memory density obeys a limit of its own

insights.claim: Communication sits only about six orders of magnitude (a factor of a million) from the Holevo limit, making it the gap the industry will likely close first.
insights.speaker: Volkan Gurses
insights.so_what: Optical interconnect efficiency is where near-term gains and investment concentrate.
insights.quote: which is the threshold the industry will likely meet first

insights.claim: Reversible or adiabatic logic can avoid the erasure energy cost, and commercial attempts have begun, with Vaire Computing testing its first chip in 2025 using resonant circuits that recover switching energy.
insights.speaker: Volkan Gurses
insights.so_what: An early-stage path to lower energy per operation, still unproven commercially.
insights.quote: the first commercial attempts are now underway

insights.claim: Nvidia and Broadcom now ship optical interconnects built right against the silicon, so signals leave the package already on photons, because interconnects are multiplying faster than the grid can power them.
insights.speaker: Volkan Gurses
insights.so_what: Co-packaged optics is the near-term energy-per-bit lever in AI data centers.
insights.quote: Nvidia and Broadcom now ship optical interconnects built right against the silicon

insights.claim: DNA stores a bit in about 30 atoms versus Feynman's guess of 125, but writing cost and speed remain many orders of magnitude from practical, so DNA storage is held back by fabrication, not physics.
insights.speaker: Volkan Gurses
insights.so_what: DNA storage is a long-dated option, not a data-center near-term story.
insights.quote: What keeps DNA storage out of the data center is not its density but the cost and speed of writing it

insights.claim: Reversible logic, quantum computing and DNA storage have each been perpetually 10 years away for 40 years, so the gap to physical limits may be a mirage in practice.
insights.speaker: Volkan Gurses
insights.so_what: Treat timelines for exotic computing paradigms with heavy skepticism.
insights.quote: have each been perpetually 10 years away for 40 years

insights.claim: Beyond the ceiling of what can be built (grid gigawatts, land, water, capital), the author argues the next machines will come from physics experiments at the floor scaled up bottom-up, as with the transistor, laser and giant magnetoresistance.
insights.speaker: Volkan Gurses
insights.so_what: Long-run advantage may go to approaches built at fundamental limits rather than incremental scaling.
insights.quote: The next machines will not be reached by descent; they will be built from the bottom up.
